unit-eng-t1-tkam.title: Test 1 · 7 To Kill a Mockingbird: Background
unit-eng-t1-tkam.source: Test 1 notes · To Kill a Mockingbird background (student’s own notes)

summary.text: Harper Lee, the small town behind Maycomb, her father’s profession and her own abandoned law degree, the 1960 publication, how the book got written, and the setting: Maycomb, Alabama, 1933 to 1935, under the Depression, legal segregation and ignorance.

why.text: This is the short, factual part of the test — the kind where every mark is available if you have the dates and the three conditions of the setting straight.

objectives.text: Name the author, the publication year, and the setting in place and time
Say how Harper Lee’s own life reaches into the novel
Name the three conditions of the 1930s that shape the book
Explain why each of those three matters to the plot
Say what the gap between the setting and the publication changes

parentNote.text: Built from Sedona’s own handwritten notes, and every factual claim on her page was checked independently — the author, the 1960 publication, the father’s profession, the abandoned law degree, the airline job, the friends who funded the writing year, and the 1933 to 1935 dating all hold up. Scoped deliberately against the reading companion she already has for chapters 1 to 5: that unit covers plot, characters and the Boo Radley material and contains none of this, so there is nothing repeated between them. Nothing here reaches past chapter five of the novel, so it is safe to approve whatever she has read so far.

nextUp.text: Short and mostly factual. Get the year, the place and the three conditions of the 1930s solid and this part is free marks.

cards.def:
**The author of To Kill a Mockingbird.**
• She published it in 1960.
• Almost everything in the novel's world comes from somewhere in her own.
cards.hint: One book, one name, one enormous reputation.

cards.term: A small town of her own
cards.def:
**She grew up in a small town, and Maycomb is based on it.**
• Maycomb itself is invented; the kind of place it is, is not.
• Knowing a town that well is why the novel's background detail is so exact.
cards.hint: She did not have to research the setting.

cards.def:
**Her father was a lawyer, and she studied law herself before dropping out to write.**
• A small-town lawyer sits at the center of the novel.
• She knew the world of a county courthouse from the inside.
cards.hint: She left the law, and then wrote about it.

cards.def:
**To Kill a Mockingbird was published in 1960.**
• It was her first novel.
• It won the Pulitzer Prize the following year.
cards.hint: 1960 — a quarter century after the events in it.

cards.def:
**She worked as an airline clerk while trying to get the book written.**
• Friends eventually gave her money so she could write full time.
• The novel exists partly because somebody funded a year of her life.
cards.hint: A day job, and then a gift that ended it.

cards.def:
**The novel is set in the invented town of Maycomb, Alabama, between 1933 and 1935.**
• Two years, one town, one county courthouse.
• Every one of the three conditions below is true of that place in those years.

**The novel is set during the Great Depression.**
• Almost nobody in Maycomb has money, and the novel says so constantly.
• Poverty is the pressure under every conflict in the book.
cards.hint: Nobody in the town has anything to spare.

cards.def:
**Segregation in the 1930s South was not merely a custom — it was written into law.**
• That is what the word “legal” is doing on your page.
• The courthouse in the novel is operating inside that system, not outside it.
cards.hint: Not just how people behaved — how the law was written.

cards.def:
**Ignorance is named as the third condition of the setting.**
• Schooling was limited, and reliable information was scarce.
• Prejudice and ignorance hold each other up, which is why both are on the list.
cards.hint: The third leg, holding the other two up.

cards.def:
**Depression, legal segregation and ignorance are the pressure the plot runs on.**
• Move the same story to another decade and most of it stops working.
• A setting question on a test is usually really a question about that pressure.
cards.hint: The setting is not scenery here. It is the engine.

cards.term: Set in the 1930s, written in the 1950s
cards.def:
**The events are 1933–1935; the book was published in 1960.**
• So it is a book looking BACK at that decade, not a report from inside it.
• Twenty-five years, and the beginning of the civil rights movement, sit in that gap.
cards.hint: A quarter of a century between the story and the telling.

questions.q: Who wrote To Kill a Mockingbird?
opts: Harper Lee
Flannery O’Connor
Eudora Welty
Carson McCullers
questions.hint: All four are Southern writers. Only one wrote this novel.
steps: Flannery O’Connor wrote short stories set in Georgia.
Eudora Welty wrote about Mississippi.
Carson McCullers wrote The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter.
To Kill a Mockingbird is Harper Lee’s.

ex.main: **Harper Lee.** The other three are real Southern writers of roughly the same era, which is worth knowing on its own — this was not a lone voice in an empty room.
ex.tip: It was her first novel, and for most of her life it was her only published one.

questions.q: In what year was To Kill a Mockingbird published?
questions.hint: It was published well after the years it describes.
steps: The novel is set between 1933 and 1935.
It was not published anywhere near those years.
Nor was it published as late as the 1970s.
It was published in 1960.

ex.main: **1960**, which is a quarter of a century after the events it describes. That gap is worth holding on to — the book looks back at the 1930s rather than reporting from inside it.
ex.tip: It won the Pulitzer Prize the year after publication.

questions.q: Where and when is the novel set?
opts: Maycomb, Georgia, 1947 to 1949
Mobile, Alabama, 1919 to 1921
Maycomb, Alabama, 1933 to 1935
Monroeville, Tennessee, 1955
questions.hint: Three of the four get either the place or the years wrong.
steps: The state is Alabama.
The town is Maycomb, which is invented.
The years are the middle of the 1930s.
Maycomb, Alabama, 1933 to 1935.

ex.main: **Maycomb, Alabama, 1933 to 1935.** Two years in one small town, and the county courthouse is at the center of them.
ex.tip: Maycomb is invented, but it is built out of a real small town the author knew.

questions.q: What was Harper Lee’s father’s profession?
opts: Teacher
Doctor
Minister
Lawyer
questions.hint: Think about the profession at the center of the novel.
steps: The novel puts a small-town lawyer at its center.
The author studied law herself before leaving to write.
That interest did not come from nowhere.
Her father was a lawyer.

ex.main: **Her father was a lawyer**, and she studied law herself before dropping out to become a writer — which is why the novel’s courthouse feels observed rather than researched.
ex.tip: Writing what you know is a cliché, but it is a fair description of what happened here.

questions.q: Harper Lee studied law and left before finishing. How does that show up in the novel?
opts: It centers on a small-town lawyer
It is narrated entirely by a judge
It quotes a statute in every chapter
It was written inside a real courtroom
questions.hint: Ask what the novel actually does with the law, not what it could have done.
steps: The novel is not narrated by a judge.
It does not quote statutes at a reader.
What it does is put a lawyer, and a trial, at its heart.
A small-town lawyer is the center of the book.

ex.main: **The novel centers on a small-town lawyer**, which is both her father’s profession and the career she started and left.
ex.tip: Knowing a world from the inside shows up as confidence in the background detail, not as legal jargon.

questions.q: Before the novel was published, how did Harper Lee support herself?
opts: By practicing law in Alabama
By working as an airline clerk
By teaching at a local school
By writing for a newspaper
questions.hint: She was not making a living from writing yet.
steps: She never finished her law degree, so she was not practicing.
She was not teaching or reporting either.
She had an ordinary job that had nothing to do with books.
She worked as an airline clerk.

ex.main: **She worked as an airline clerk** while trying to get the book written — a detail worth keeping, because it says something true about how long books take.
ex.tip: The job ended when friends gave her money to write full time.

questions.q: What let Harper Lee stop working and write full time?
opts: A university research grant
The success of an earlier novel
A gift of money from friends
A contract to write a screenplay
questions.hint: It was not the book that paid for the book.
steps: This was her first novel, so no earlier one had made money.
No university or studio was involved.
The money came from people who knew her.
Friends gave her money so she could write full time.

ex.main: **Friends funded a year of her life so she could finish it.** The novel exists partly because somebody decided it was worth paying for before anyone had read a word.
ex.tip: Worth remembering next time a book seems to have appeared out of nowhere.

questions.q: Which set names the three conditions of the 1930s that shape the novel?
opts: Prohibition, radio, and drought
War, rationing, and migration
Industry, immigration, and growth
Depression, segregation, ignorance
questions.hint: All four sets describe real features of some part of American history.
steps: Rationing and mass migration belong to the 1940s.
Industry and immigration describe a different era and a different region.
Prohibition had ended by 1933.
The three named conditions are the Great Depression, prejudice with legal segregation, and ignorance.

ex.main: **The Great Depression, prejudice and legal segregation, and ignorance.** These three are not background colour — they are the pressure the whole plot runs on.
ex.tip: Move the same story to a wealthier decade and most of it stops working.

questions.q: Maycomb is invented, but it is built out of something real. What?
opts: The small town the author grew up in
A town she read about in a court record
A city she moved to as a grown adult
A town invented for an earlier novel
questions.hint: She did not need to research what a small Alabama town was like.
steps: This was her first novel, so there is no earlier one to borrow from.
She did not build it from documents or from a city.
She grew up in a small Southern town herself.
Maycomb is based on the town she grew up in.

ex.main: **Maycomb is invented, and the kind of place it is is not.** That is why its background detail — who knows whom, who owes whom, what everybody has always said — reads as observed.
ex.tip: Inventing the name gave her freedom; knowing the real place gave her the detail.

questions.q: The novel describes 1933 to 1935 but was published in 1960. Why does that gap matter?
opts: It was written while those events happened
It looks back on the 1930s from later
It means the dates inside it are unreliable
It shows the author never visited Alabama
questions.hint: Twenty-five years is long enough for the country to have changed.
steps: A book published in 1960 was not written during 1933.
The dates inside the novel are perfectly clear.
The author grew up in Alabama, so she certainly visited.
The novel is looking back across twenty-five years at a decade that was already over.

ex.main: **It is a book about the past, written later, for readers living in a changed country.** The beginning of the civil rights movement sits inside that twenty-five-year gap.
ex.tip: A novel written from inside the 1930s would have been a different book entirely.

questions.q: Why does the Great Depression matter to a story about one small Alabama town?
opts: It is the reason the novel has a narrator
It explains why the town has no school
Poverty sharpens every conflict in it
It places the story outside the South
questions.hint: Think about what having no money does to a disagreement between neighbours.
steps: The town does have a school; that is not what the Depression explains.
Every novel has a narrator, Depression or not.
The Depression does not move the story anywhere.
What it does is put every person in the town under financial pressure.

ex.main: **Poverty is the pressure under every conflict in the book.** When nobody has anything to spare, ordinary disagreements get harder and pride gets more expensive.
ex.tip: The setting here is not scenery — it is closer to being the engine.

questions.q: Segregation in the 1930s South is described as LEGAL. What does that word add?
opts: It had already ended by the mid-1930s
It only applied inside actual courtrooms
It was enforced by one county judge alone
The unfairness was written into the law
questions.hint: Compare a rule people follow out of habit with a rule a court will enforce.
steps: It had not ended — it lasted decades longer.
It was not the decision of any single judge.
It reached far beyond courtrooms into schools, buses and shops.
Legal means the system itself required it, rather than merely tolerating it.

ex.main: **Legal segregation means the unfairness was the law, not a departure from it.** That is why a trial in this novel is happening inside the system rather than against it.
ex.tip: It is the difference between breaking the rules and the rules themselves being the problem.
